# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

founder.order_why: Context, then problem, then delivery is the right arc, but the window question (4) sits between two identical context screens (3 and 5), so the context step reads as interrupted and then restarted.

founder.missing: Nothing asks about the setting where the conversation was lost (dinner table, bar, theatre, work meeting, counter behind a mask), and that is where my wedge lives. The flow also never reaches the glasses (phone plus internet), the price ($599 to $839 a year) or who pays (HSA/FSA), so the solution and commercial side goes untested.

PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what kind of conversation it was or where (a noisy restaurant, a group, at work, a show) or what I did when I lost the thread, like lip-reading, asking people to repeat, writing things down, or just giving up and nodding along or leaving. screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: Frequency is exactly at the bar (4 of 6) and only 7 people answered, so before leaning on 'most days' ask a few more people how many days a week they lose the thread.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I see the verdict and the count that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip is seven cells, all for me, on a 0 to 7 axis with the marker at 6 labelled "at least 8 in 10", so what's counted, over how many and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The band "At least 8 in 10" and the gate's clause are mine, but my segment is cut to "deaf or hard-of-hearing adults", dropping "in the US who talk with hearing people every week", and the Asked line carries a stray "— the most recent time it happened" the gate never asked.
screens.why_b4: "Common among these 7" plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me where to look, but not what this means for AirCaps, for instance that how many people have the problem isn't the risk in my wedge.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, says "a small group: a lean, not a call" and limits the claim to "these 7", so it claims nothing beyond the people who answered.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up, with 4 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6 right beside it, and 'at the bar' ties the number to the verdict.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7 over 6 counted with the marker at 4 is readable, but it takes a second look: the axis starts at 0, which nobody could answer, and the legend's 'at what you said' next to 'what you said' is unclear.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and 'lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people on 4 to 7 days out of 7' are my range and my people's words for what happens at the table.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' only sends me on; it does not say that a pass exactly at the bar, with 2 of 6 at 1 to 3 days, means my 4-to-7 claim is borderline and I should test the lower end.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a lean, not a call', but the headline still says Holding up for a pass exactly at the bar on 6 people, and 'the most recent time it happened' under a question that counts days across a week misdescribes what was asked.
screens.instead: At the bar, just: 4 of 6 lose the thread 4+ days a week and 2 only 1 to 3, so with 6 people this is a lean; check whether your heavy users skew to the 4-to-7 end before you build on daily use.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 6 put it in their two and bar 4 of 6, so I know the belief held and by what count.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 6 people each picked two and the bars count 12 picks, my row is marked as the problem I named at 6, and the strip puts all 6 cells past the marker at 4.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, with my own item and my four other rows; only the question's occasion, 'last day out and about', is not the group conversation I had in mind.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly warns that top two is not first place, but it never says what this means for AirCaps, for example that 3 of 6 also picked getting a word in, the 'join' half of my job.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Harriet out as a guess), the small group is called a lean, not a call, and the So line refuses to claim it ranks first.
screens.instead: All 6 put following what hearing people say in their two, a lean from a small group; getting a word in came next for 3 of 6, so captions alone may not cover the 'join' half: check whether people want help speaking up too.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6', and the strip shows 5 for and 1 against with the marker at 4, so the number plainly decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each of my five rungs carries its count and its for or against, my line sits under 'Missed a little, caught up quickly', and the strip shows the 6 counted against a bar of 4, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief line and the rung named in the bar are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line names the gap concretely (3 got the gist but missed details, 2 lost the thread and nodded along), but 'judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic hand-off and doesn't say what the gap means for AirCaps.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Harriet's guess left out), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the So line keeps the claim to 'these 6'.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 5 of these 6, and mostly in the details: 3 caught the gist but missed what was said, 2 nodded along. On the next study, test whether captions in the lenses give back the details, not just the gist.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on Holding up with 5 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6 right beside it, and the line 'Current solution held, 5 of 6; the 1 who said no' ties the verdict to its number.
screens.why_b3: Current solution and my belief about hearing aids or phone captions falling short are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what the one dissent means for the idea, for example that people with one-sided or mild loss who can manage by choosing their seat are a weaker part of my segment.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay visible and modest, but a lone quote under 'what keeps today's way working' with only n=6 is not flagged as a single voice, and the stray 'Missed a little, caught up quickly / against' fragment after it reads as an unexplained label.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat workaround for single-sided deafness is something I did not type: a coping trick that marks the edge of my segment and a reason some will not pay $599.
screens.instead: Say: 1 of 6 manages today, a person deaf on one side who takes the end seat; people with one-sided or mild loss may not need the glasses, so check whether that group belongs in your wedge.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is plainly a gate, checking that I am someone who deals with hearing people week to week before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and other deaf people talk about everyone else, so I would answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I talked with hearing people this week, at the shops, at work or with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a gate question rightly has no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment words almost word for word, and nothing about a product or a company's terms for me leaks through.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and a yes or no, easy to hold on one hearing, though "I'll read 2 options" is a bit stiff for a plain yes or no.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I lost track of one of those conversations this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread" is exactly how I'd describe it: the moment I stop following who's saying what and start nodding along.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me this week, at the shop counter, at work or at dinner with friends.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips about not recalling one or not wanting to say belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, captions or the company reaches me; it asks only about something that happened to me, in words I'd use.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short sentence ending in "Yes or no," easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the costly outcome (losing the thread), not the circumstance every one of us is in, so a week of quiet one-to-one talks gives a true No and a noisy group chat gives a true Yes, with no escape on the gate, as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I lost the thread this week, it's natural to ask how many days that happened.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread" is exactly how I'd put it when I'm with hearing people and suddenly can't follow, so I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I know which days I was at the shop, at work or with family and missed what was being said, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button for each day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer after a yes, with no overlap, and "I can't recall" fits if the week is a blur.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan comes through; it's just about my week talking with hearing people.
screens.why6: It's one short question, then "say a number from 1 to 7" and the escape, which is easy to take in at once, though on a call I'd need it captioned like any spoken question.
screens.why7: Every option counts days out of the 7-day window, from 1 to 7 in order with no 0 and no bands, the unit is named once, and the one required escape is there, so a founder's range starting at 2 or more can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which of the hard things I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: Every option is in words I'd use myself, and I'd get it on first reading.
screens.why3: I deal with all of these myself in a normal week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Phone and video calls overlap with following what hearing people say. 'Not being worn out by listening' reads backwards after 'made easier', and for me it's lipreading more than listening.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is following and joining a conversation face to face, but here 'following' and 'getting a word in' are split into two rows and 'face to face' has gone.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options I can hold in my head, with 'none of these' said last.
screens.why7: The founder's own item is there and none is first, so the belief can go either way, but the own row is narrowed to following only. Its other half is made into a rival, and the phone and video row is another channel, which the card warns against.
screens.instead: Think of your last day out and about. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up with and joining a conversation face to face · Catching announcements in shops and stations · Getting people to face me when they talk · Not ending the day worn out from lipreading · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread and what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Phone captions' and 'hearing aids' are plain to me, but tying two tools into the question makes me stop: what if I used one, both or neither, and lipread most of it?
screens.why3: I know how my last conversation went, but not everyone like me uses hearing aids or captions every time, so some of us would have to guess how to fit our real way into the question.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from following nearly everything to not following at all, each is distinct and in words I'd use ('nodded along' is exactly what I do), and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the tool list reads like someone's notes on what we use today, pasted into the question, rather than how I'd describe my own way.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list, but 'how did following the conversation with hearing aids or phone captions go' is a mouthful heard once, with 'conversation' twice in one breath.
screens.why7: The measure is one scale of how well I followed, there are five options best to worst with a working first rung and outright failure last, the belief can go either way, and the escape is the right one for an act no one can do for me; but the stem carries a method, a two-tool list, which the card's item rule and pitfalls forbid.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How well did you follow it? -- Followed nearly everything said · Missed a little, caught up quickly · Caught the gist, missed the details · Lost the thread and mostly nodded along · Could not follow it at all · or I can't recall
